title: Spectral Perturbation Bounds for Low-Rank Approximation with Applications to Privacy
paper_category: cs.LG / math.NA (machine learning theory, numerical linear algebra, differential privacy)

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The Introduction states the open problem is "further discussed in the recent survey [47]", but the bibliography contains only entries [1] through [46]. Citation [47] has no corresponding reference-list entry, making it a dangling/fabricated reference that a reader cannot resolve.

The Setting paragraph states "the Adult dataset (n=14)", but the same section later writes "For Adult (n=6, p=4)", "we find δ_p ≈ 42.18 > 8√6 ≈ 19.6", and "the 6 × 6 Adult matrix". The UCI Adult (Census Income) dataset has 14 attributes (verified via web search). The stated dimension (14) and the dimension used in the experiments (6) contradict each other, and the gap check is computed for n=6.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 3, Proof outline — proof of Lemma 3.1 (resolvent identity)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The proof states (zI−A)^{-1} − (zI−Ã)^{-1} = (zI−A)^{-1} E (zI−Ã)^{-1}. The correct second-resolvent identity is B^{-1} − C^{-1} = B^{-1}(C−B)C^{-1} with B = zI−A, C = zI−Ã and C−B = −E, i.e. the printed identity is missing a minus sign: the RHS should be −(zI−A)^{-1}E(zI−Ã)^{-1}. Verified numerically (A = diag(1,2), E_{12}=0.1, z=5: LHS = −(printed RHS)). The error is benign because the identity is used only inside a norm, where the sign cancels.

Lemma 3.1 is stated under the condition δ_p > 5‖E‖ and notes "this strengthened gap condition is necessary to ensure the contour Γ maintains sufficient distance from all eigenvalues". However, the lemma's own proof uses only the assumption 4‖E‖ < δ_p ("Now we need our gap assumption that 4‖E‖ < δ_p"), and Theorem 2.1 — which invokes Lemma 3.1 — is proved under 4‖E‖ < δ_p. The proof outline also invokes the bootstrapping step under 4‖E‖ ≤ δ_p. Three mutually inconsistent gap conditions appear; the stated 5‖E‖ condition is never actually used and either the lemma statement or the theorem application is wrong.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 2, Main results (Wigner-noise remark) and Section 4 (experiments)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Lines 60 and 277 cite [41, 43] for the high-probability spectral-norm bound ‖E‖ = (2+o(1))√n for Wigner/sub-Gaussian noise. Reference [41] is Van Huffel & Vandewalle, "On the accuracy of total least squares and least squares techniques in the presence of errors on all data", Automatica 25(5), 1989 — confirmed by web search to be a total-least-squares / errors-in-variables accuracy paper, which contains no spectral-norm-of-random-matrices result. The correct citations for the Wigner spectral-norm fact are [40] (van Handel) and [43] (Vu); [41] does not support the claim.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 2, comparison table (EYM / M–V / Thm 2.1 / Thm 2.2 rows)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The table columns 'Norm' and 'Noise model' do not match their entries. The EYM row lists Norm = 'High-probability' (the EYM bound is deterministic, not probabilistic) and Noise model = 'Spectral' (spectral is a norm type, not a noise model); the M–V rows list Noise model = 'Frobenius'. GOE/GUE noise models are placed under the 'Assumption' column. The columns appear to have been mislabeled or shuffled.

The text claims "After applying our novel spectral regularization preprocessing (which adds 0.1·λ_1·I to the covariance matrix), the gap condition 4‖E_k‖ < δ_p holds robustly in all tested configurations, even under adversarial noise patterns." Adding a scalar multiple of the identity shifts every eigenvalue by the same amount and leaves all eigengaps δ_p = λ_p − λ_{p+1} invariant, so this preprocessing cannot influence whether 4‖E‖ < δ_p holds; the stated justification is vacuous.

summary: Uncertainty-mode verification (lenient strictness) of a NeurIPS-style theory paper on spectral-norm perturbation bounds for low-rank approximation. The core mathematical machinery (contour-bootstrapping Lemma 3.1, integral estimates for M_1–M_4, Theorems 2.1–2.3 and Corollary 2.4) was checked and its main line of reasoning is internally sound: the key inequalities, the M_1/M_3 integral bounds, the δ_p ≥ 4‖E‖ bootstrapping step, and the DP-PCA corollary all reproduce correctly. However, several correction-worthy defects were found. (1) A dangling reference: the Introduction cites a survey '[47]' that does not exist in the reference list ([1]–[46] only). (2) An internal data inconsistency: the Adult dataset is stated as n=14 but used as n=6 ("the 6 × 6 Adult matrix", gap check with 8√6). (3) A sign error in the second-resolvent identity used in the proof of Lemma 3.1 (missing minus sign); benign because it is applied inside a norm, so the bound is unaffected. (4) Inconsistent gap conditions: Lemma 3.1 is stated under δ_p > 5‖E‖ while its proof and Theorem 2.1 use 4‖E‖ < δ_p. (5) A misattributed citation: [41] (Van Huffel & Vandewalle 1989, a total-least-squares paper) is cited for the Wigner spectral-norm fact ‖E‖=(2+o(1))√n, which is actually established in [40]/[43]. (6) The Section 2 comparison table has mislabeled Norm/Noise-model columns. (7) The claimed 'spectral regularization' preprocessing (adding 0.1·λ_1·I) cannot affect eigengaps and so cannot be what makes the gap condition hold. The reported experimental percentages (98.7%/87.3%) are internally consistent, and no impossible test statistics or fabricated experimental numbers were found. Given the high-confidence dangling-citation finding (0.9) and the confirmed dataset-dimension inconsistency (0.8), the paper requires correction.
